We will begin our work. Your Excellency, Pedro Sanchez, Head of the Government of Spain, distinguished Heads of State and Government, distinguished Ministers, distinguished representatives of observers, United Nations system entities, and other accredited intergovernmental organizations, as well as civil society representatives, excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. I call to order the fifth multi-stakeholder roundtable. of the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development. The theme of the roundtable is Realizing a Development-Oriented Sovereign Debt Architecture. At the outset, I would like to wish you a very warm welcome. For me, It is a great honor to be co-chairing this multi-stakeholder roundtable together with His Excellency, Mr. Pedro Sanchez, head of the government of Spain. The summary of today's discussions will be submitted to the closing plenary meeting of the conference held on Thursday afternoon on the 3rd of July. Before we proceed, I would like to make some introductory remarks about the theme of our discussion today. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, I would like to thank you all for participating in this roundtable on a very important topic. It is of concern to all States but particularly worrisome for developing countries. Debt sustainability requires us to address the fact that not only is there unproductive spending, but there are also rules which are not aligned with our long-term objectives. Realizing a development-oriented sovereign debt architecture is something we've been striving for for a long time now. But this is now a pressing matter given the multiple crises weakening our economies and exacerbating inequality. Too many countries are faced with a conundrum, either honoring their debt commitments or investing in priority sectors such as education, health, access to water, sanitation and agriculture, necessary for them to be able to feed their people. This trade-off is unacceptable. It's too difficult for the human conscience to bear. Therefore, we must go down the path of sustainable development that exhibits solidarity. This requires us to take action. Not just in terms of sovereign debt architecture reform, but this reform is necessary and it must be underpinned by various pillars. First, justice. By guaranteeing equitable treatment of both public and private creditors, and by agreeing on fairer restructuring mechanisms that are also more predictable, Well, this would require a multilateral mechanism for orderly treatment of sovereign debt. The next thing we need is transparency in order to prevent excessive debt burdens and to restore markets' trust and confidence. Third, a revision of credit rating agencies' systems. to ensure better access to lending, to borrowing conditions and reimbursement conditions. Next, addressing shocks and recognizing the historic climate burden which is weighing on developing countries. It is high time that we recognize that these pillars are already reflected in the civil commitment with a view to bolstering financing for development. This sends a positive signal, but we have a long way to go. Africa cannot continue to face all of these constraints, living off promises. Africa must be a vehicle for solutions. We stand ready to shoulder our responsibilities. On our side, Senegal, intends to bolster debt management discipline, to improve budgetary transparency, and to ensure that any external borrowing results in a collective return on investment. Furthermore, my country will continue advocating for bold, inclusive, bold and inclusive reforms that are geared towards achieving the SDGs. Such reforms would ensure that finance serves the people and not vice versa. I thank you. I will now hand over to my fellow co-chair, His Excellency Pedro Sanchez, head of the government of Spain. He will be delivering a keynote address. I thank you.

Thank you, President. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, dear friends. I think that the consensus that is emerging today in Seville is unambiguous. That is that the weight of sovereign debt is suffocating many developing countries. In a context of successive crises, natural disasters, pandemics and climate shocks, debt has become one of the greatest obstacles to sustainable development. The data here is clear, but also very painful. Since 2010, public debt has grown twice as quickly in developing countries than in developed economies. The public external debt of developing countries has reached a record level of $3.3 trillion, and half of developing countries dedicate at least 8.6% of their public income to servicing their external debt. 3.4 billion people live in countries that spend more on paying their debt interest than on health and education together. And against this backdrop, I'd like to propose three areas of action that should guide our common response. Firstly, we should bolster debt relief and restructuring mechanisms. It's unacceptable that those countries suffering a crisis spend years wallowing in them. But this means that we need to improve the, resolutely improve the G20 common framework. We need to do so quickly, effectively, resolving once and for all. the issues to ensure that creditors are treated equally and more inclusively for that so that middle income countries can also benefit from it. An important and innovative proposal that we've suggested that could help the most heavily indebted countries is introducing debt payment suspension clauses where there are crises, be they health, food or climate crises, as well as debt for sustainable investment swaps. Spain has promoted specific initiatives in both areas, reflected in the Sevilla Platform for Action. We have the partnership for debt service suspension clauses and the global hub for debt swaps, and we invite all the other countries to join these. Secondly, I'd like to highlight that it's important to recognize the fact that we need to find new ways to assess debt sustainability. Spain advocates for there to be more information and more transparency, like the President of Senegal said, both for creditors and borrowers, but also to ensure more thorough long term assessments that should better integrate investments in resilience, nature and productive capacities. Definitively, we need to be able to more clearly distinguish between liquidity problems and solvency problems, and we need to be able to not penalize those that are restructuring their debt in an orderly way or investing in the future. Because what we can't do is allow it to become normal for developing countries to pay three times more for their external debt than developed countries. The third and last way is to mobilize more domestic resources. No country can invest in its own development if it's not able to collect and sufficiently correctly use its resources. This goes for low-income economies, but also for some advanced economies where, despite reasonable growth rates, deficits are shooting up, sometimes shoot up due to irresponsible fiscal decisions that compromise trust in sovereign debt. We believe that the debt agenda is intimately linked to the fiscal agenda. Therefore, we are in favor of establishing some minimum thresholds for tax collection depending on GDP. And also, we think we should be designing more efficient... tax systems that are fairer and more progressive. We need to have more political will to ensure that every country is contributing as it can. So we're also going to be implementing the two pillar solution that was adopted within the G20, so that, and the OECD, so that great multi, the big multinationals pay tax where they really generate value. We also need to ensure fair taxation of the most wealthy. This is something that we've already kicked off in the G20 and we can't go back on what we've done there. The initiative that we put together, put forward in the Seville Platform for Action is the best demonstration of our commitment here. Finally, we need to bring an end to tax havens, because while they exist, there will continue to be companies and... wealthy individuals who continue to benefit while millions of people continue not to have access to basic services, education or health. I conclude by saying that the Seville Commitment doesn't resolve all the challenges, but it does establish a specific roadmap to transform the way that we manage debt in the 21st century, because well-managed debt is a development tool, but poorly managed debt, it is a trap that perpetuates poverty. So, in Spain, we are committed to working with all of you so that this roadmap begets real change, so that debt stops being an obstacle and finally becomes a lever of progress. That's all. Thank you very much.

I would like to thank my fellow co-chair for those remarks. We will now hear a number of special addresses. I have the honor of inviting His Excellency Gaston Brown, Prime Minister of Antigua and Barbuda, to address the roundtable. Prime Minister, you have the floor.

Thank you very much, co-chairs, Excellencies, distinguished ladies and gentlemen. At the adoption of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS, the Abbas, We define this decade from 2024 to 2034 as the most decisive in shaping the future of small island developing states. For too long, our small islands, many of them microstates, have struggled against overwhelming odds. The climate crisis, social upheavals like the pandemic, and above all, our deep economic vulnerability compounded by a growing debt crisis, have placed our development and our very survival at risk. The ABAS is our blueprint to change that trajectory. It is bold, comprehensive, and forward-looking. And here in Seville at FFD4, we have a historic opportunity to align global financing frameworks with the needs of SIDS and turn that vision into reality. Let me be clear. For many of our nations, the road to debt sustainability cannot wait. Our economies face crushing debt service burdens, high borrowing costs, and narrowing fiscal space. These conditions suffocate our ability to respond to shocks, invest in people, and pursue our sustainable development goals. To address this, I offer six key proposals for urgent action. each grounded in the ABAS and reinforced by the FFD4 outcome document. Firstly, to operationalize the Debt Sustainability Support Service, the DSSS. Reference in paragraph 76D of the outcome, the DSSS offers the legal and technical support SIDS need to manage debt and climate risk. It should be recognized as the principal delivery tool for the ABAS debt commitments. and integrated into the WBG's small states approach. The second issue is to address currency volatility and expand local currency lending. Too many states are penalized by external debt denominated in foreign currencies, paying up to 35% more due to FX fluctuations. This undermines predictability and resilience. FFD4 calls and MDBs to expand local currency lending, and this must be fast-tracked. The third is to implement the Multi-dimensional Vulnerability Index, the MVI. After 30 years of advocacy, we have consensus on the MVI. Let us be a fact now. The MVI must be our guide to access grants, concessional finance, and post-disaster support. based not on outdated income measures, but on real vulnerability. The fourth issue is to reform the credit rating methodologies. Current systems unfairly penalize SIDS for size, import dependence, and exposure to climate shocks, adding up to 4% to our borrowing costs. This deters investment in adaptation and resilience. We must develop a resilience rating framework aligned with the MVI and climate risk indicators. The fifth issue is to scale up blue economy financing. The Abbas recognizes the blue economy as central to our prosperity. Let us scale up instruments like debt for nature swaps, marine investments, and blue bonds supported through the new WBG facilities dedicated to blue resilience. And the sixth, is to operationalize the SIDS Center of Excellence. Outlined in the ABAS, the center will serve as a hub for data, innovation, and coordinated investment. We invite the WBG and partners to support its data platform, early warning systems, and project pipeline development. Colleagues, despite repeated calls, most SIDS remain excluded from existing debt relief mechanisms. due to the outdated GNI classifications. We must design new tailored instruments to include cancellation, rescheduling, debt for climate swaps, the materialities SIDS face. This is not a new conversation. For decades, SIDS have put forward practical solutions. Now is the moment to act. If we are serious about this being a decisive decade, then we must stop talking and start implementing. The debt crisis must be resolved urgently. Without that, there is no path to growth, no resilience, and certainly no sustainability. Finally, let us remember, SIDS contribute significantly to the global commons, from marine biodiversity to early warning systems and blue carbon sinks. We are stewards of 30% of the world's oceans. That moral responsibility deserves tangible support. We therefore urge major donors and institutions to link investments in SIDS to global public goods, from food security to climate surveillance, and deliver fairer, more concessional terms for countries that carry so much yet ask for so little. Thank you, Chair. It's now my honor to invite Mr. Professor Joseph Stiglitz, the Nobel Prize Laureate for Economy, to give his keynote statement.

Well, I want to begin by thanking Spain and the UN for bringing us all together at a moment of global solidarity in advancing a set of shared values at a time of such turmoil. I want to begin by emphasizing that one needs to look at finance for development comprehensively. All actions which provide more revenues, especially hard currencies, and all actions which decrease the outflow of funds should be on the table. Of course, a major source of outflows that has already been described are those associated with servicing the debt. Excessive debt is the joint responsibility of debtors and creditors, but especially of creditors, because they are typically the ones that are supposed to have expertise in risk management. The global debt and finance architecture is also central, and it's been clear that it's not fit for purpose. It has resulted repeatedly in excessive debts, which lead to lower growth and real hardship. The debt restructurings that follow have been marked by too little and too late. The Jubilee Commission, appointed by the late Pope Francis, and which I have had the honor to chair, identified several underlying causes. A system that amplifies crises and makes them more frequent. The first is the lack of an effective architecture for dealing with sovereign debt crises. No bankruptcy courts as there are in the case of domestic debt. Secondly, there's a lack of affordable long-term finance for development. Debt is not inherently bad. In fact, sustainable credit can promote infrastructure investment and economic transformation. Financing for development requires that the global system must shift from short-term speculative flows towards long-term productive finance. That underscores the importance of scaling up concessional lending for the low-income countries and financing from multilateral development banks to the developing countries. It also requires empowering countries to mobilize domestic resources and develop local currency capital markets and imposing regulations that discourage destabilizing speculative short-term capital flows. Thirdly, overall, a pro-cyclical of global financial flows to developing countries shifts the burden of risk onto them and in turn results in the fourth problem, an unfair cost of capital. Indeed, markets and credit rating agencies routinely exaggerate the risks facing African countries and other developing countries, charging interest rates well in excess of that needed to compensate for the risk of nonpayment. The Jubilee Commission identified short-term and long-term actions, some easy, some hard, that can be undertaken by all stakeholders, reflecting the shared responsibility and shared interest. And many of these have been reflected in the Seville agenda. For instance, actions by the countries in which most of the credit originates, changing laws which have perverse incentives in resolving debt crises would make a big difference. A commitment by the IMF and the international community not to bail out private creditors, as is happening today de facto. There are negative flows from the private sector, that is, the private sector is taking back money. These flows are enabled by the international financial institutions providing money to the developing countries that was supposed to promote economic development, but it's being used instead simply to pay off the private creditors. Reflecting the comprehensive approach I have urged, we also need to think about tax reforms, changing investment agreements which have imposed huge liabilities on certain countries. We need to reform the trade architecture, which, contrary to certain assertions, has been advantaging the U.S. and certain other advanced countries at the expense of developing countries. We need to ensure that developing countries get fair value for their natural resources, to stop the flow of illicit funds, which is costing developing countries so much, and for which the safe harbors provided by developed countries are so responsible. And finally, we need to use all the tools in our toolkit, including SDRs, both new issuances and re-channeling existing issuances by a coalition of the willing. I believe that the Seville Conference will be remembered as a launchpad for further action, especially to the Seville Action Platform. President Sanchez has outlined a whole set of particular items that can be done. Every one of these, I think, is meaningful, are practical, and Each of them would make a big difference. Together, they would make a huge difference. These ideas overlap with many of the recommendations of the Jubilee Commission. For the full impact of the Civil Action Platform to be realized, we must continue to push for more ambitious yet feasible solutions, for example, Creating a Jubilee Fund with 100 billion worth of untapped SDRs for debt buybacks would provide the most vulnerable countries with resources that they desperately need to promote sustainable growth. Equally, one can imagine broader frameworks for debt for nature and debt for development swaps. as well as new and fairer green trade investment agreements that enhance domestic resources and facilitate developing countries' participation in the global effort to address climate change. In concluding, Seville represents an opportunity to look at finance comprehensively and send a strong message of commitment, of optimism, and trust in multilateralism. Thank you.

We advocate for an ambitious redefinition of the concept of public debt sustainability. The latter can no longer be assessed solely through repayment capacity or budgetary balances. It must integrate the effective contribution of debt to financing sustainable development, economic resilience and social cohesion. Debt is sustainable if it creates wealth, if it transforms the economy and if it ensures a more inclusive future for future generations. Despite a restrictive international environment, Tunisia has stabilized its public debt level at around 80% of our GDP, with a gradual reduction in external debt to around 43%. This development has notably been driven by increased recourse to financing on the domestic bank, that's local bank, domestic market, that's local banks, and the central bank. reflecting a strategy of sovereign re-anchoring and controlling our external risks. However, this rebalancing is accompanied by urgent investment needs in strategic sectors to ensure sustainable, green and inclusive growth. We continue to face challenges, calling for widespread investment in the following areas. Firstly, the energy transition, developing renewable energy and regional electrical interconnections, modernizing the rail and urban transport networks. Secondly, adaptation to climate change, water management, transforming the agricultural sector, decarbonizing the economy, youth employment, and reducing regional inequalities. So, We need to redirect debt flows towards structuring projects with a strong socioeconomic impact. Debt shouldn't finance the functioning of the state, but rather serve to build the country's human, technological, and environmental infrastructure. Tunisia calls for systematic prioritization of value-adding projects that generate jobs and that have high social and environmental returns. In terms of the current eligibility criteria for concessional financing, these remain inadequate for the needs of middle-income countries like Tunisia. These criteria are mainly based on per capita income or macroeconomic aggregates. This obscures structural vulnerabilities and transformation needs. Tunisia supports a fair review of the criteria for access to concessional financing, taking into account the following. Firstly, climate and social vulnerability. Secondly, absorption and implementation capacities. And three, the potential for long-term transformation. In light of the increasing frequency of exogenous shocks, natural disasters, soaring commodity prices, geopolitical tensions, et cetera, Tunisia is calling for the institutionalization of debt suspension or debt relief mechanisms in the event of a major crisis. We also support the establishment of insurance instruments that insure against sovereign risks, as well as the integration of flexibility clauses in public debt contracts. As by way of conclusion, debt shouldn't be perceived as a constraint, but as a strategic lever for transformation. For countries like Tunisia, sustainability must rhyme with development, equity, and resilience. Tunisia reaffirms its commitment to a fairer, more inclusive sovereign debt architecture focused on investment in human capital, the green transition, and regional integration. And we agree with that. You should delink this from the GNI classification. We have done it. We have made most of these countries IDA-eligible, and we are providing about $200 per capita for the CITS. That is up from $85 seven years ago. And if you compare it to the IDA universe, it is four times what the IDA universe gets. So there is a recognition of this problem. Then the next point, the third is when there is problem, and when I said there should be positive flows, creditors need to stay engaged. That can be a rollover, it can be also new money, but it cannot be withdrawn because it exacerbates the situation, and we need to work for that. And finally, we need to promote radical debt transparency. Actors need to know what the situation is. Governments should publish what they contract, let the domestic universe, the parliaments, the journalists, the civil society discuss how the situation is, and on that basis, decide how that can best serve development and not that it can be a cause for debt distress. Thank you.

Thank you so much. You highlighted many important things and it's good that you managed to have great responses to issues raised, especially by the two heads of state. And your point on solvency and how it's being treated and the liquidation issues. But can I exploit part of the stock of friendship and a couple of things? Two pointed questions. On the inclusion of middle-income countries in the common framework, did you articulate a you along with the IMF in getting the middle income countries as part of the common framework.

I think countries that are facing solvency, we can be in it. It is a question if countries choose that. I know from some countries they have opted for alternative ways. So that is basically up to the countries to decide, but this is one way of dealing with it.

Yeah, but So far, the creditors are only entertaining the request coming from low income countries and the middle income countries are not qualified. That's why Sri Lanka had as a middle income country, its own way.
Sri Lanka could have asked for the action.

Okay, so let's hear it as well from the rest of the team here. Can I come back to one more question about the excellent work the IMF and the World Bank is doing now in the consultation on the debt sustainability analysis. You managed to tell us something about the importance of time. When we can really expect the conclusion of the reform of the current DSA for the low-income countries? Are you willing to help as well in supporting the IMF in the work related to the one with market access, if it is going to be reformed as well?

I think with the DSA, this is a process where we have made an effort to be as conclusive as possible. So, Mahmoud, because you need to listen. What we would like to have is a consultative process that ultimately can be carried by the membership, and that is our interest on this. We have done extensive work on this. There are difficult issues to be addressed. It is not only the external debt, it is also the domestic debt, and these are critical issues which then affect also the big principles underlying debt restructuring, like equity of treatment.

Right. Thank you so much. I didn't mean to interrupt the flow of your good answer, but I had guidance now just from the secretary that the co-chairs have some time constraints. And so I'll turn it back to you and then we'll continue the discussion with your permission after that. So, yeah. All right, okay. Thank you so much for your time, co-chairs. All right, can I now ask, please, Remy Rieu, the AFD CEO and chairman of Finance and Common Coalition, to take the floor for three minutes or less. Thank you.

Co-chairs, Excellencies, I speak today on behalf of the Finance in Common System, the global coalition of all 530 public development banks in the world, international, regional and national, which together channel more than 2.5 trillion US dollar in public investments each year, representing roughly 50% of total global investments. I will not comment on debt restructuring mechanisms. We, of course, support clear procedures and fair treatment of all creditors, relying on IMF and World Bank mandates. I want to stress, probably with Jay Collins, the importance and possibility of sustainable, fair, and responsible lending, especially in a context of severe cuts in ODA and debt stress in many countries. We are honored that the effort of finance in common are explicitly recognized and encouraged in the Sevilla outcome document. We feel responsible to do more and to do better now individually and as a collective system based on our complementarities to originate way more projects, innovate and scale up sustainable development investments. To help countries surpass and avoid debt crisis, public development banks, if properly regulated, can provide long-term quality counter-cyclical financing when market-based finance is not there yet or retreats. We support inserting climate-resilient debt clauses in our contract. We can deploy public mandates to the last mile, leveraging SDR or mobilizing carbon markets. Public development banks also channel private finance in a sustainable way. We propose today to work with investors to define what could be a new PDB asset class with dedicated criteria and governance. The discussion has started with Team Europe and the Green Climate Fund. This is the Global Green Bond Initiative, and is also ongoing with MIGA and the World Bank Group to lower the cost of capital. There are only 100 public development banks issuing bonds for now. We propose to double that number by 2030, focusing on national development banks. I ask all the parties to support our work. Compared to a decade ago, PDBs have now structured and could become the public backbone of a more coherent, inclusive, and sustainable financial system. The next steps for finance in common is to transform the 530 public development banks from a fragmented architecture into a coordinated system with the right standards relying on each other, bridging public and private finance, development and climate, and global ambitions with local realities. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Mr. Riu, and we appreciate what you are doing, especially through the network of the MDBs and what you are doing as well in reimagining the future of official development assistance with more impact and more partnerships to support countries and provide as well active solutions on the debt challenges that we are facing. So last but not least in this round, we have Jay Collins, the Vice Chairman of Citigroup. Jay, the floor is yours.

Thank you, co-chairs and excellencies. First, I want to applaud the Compromiso de Sevilla, which includes a plethora of recommendations from an extraordinary group of private sector organizations and leaders that many of us hope and believe, if taken, would crowd in more capital into the developing countries where it is so needed. While the GSDR and the G7 have worked on much needed reforms to the common framework, up until today, it has violated the most important and basic rule of sovereign restructuring to deliver a speedy, transparent, and clear route to recovery. Speed here is the operative word, and it is the most critical of all missing ingredients. So regardless of your views on the technical debt restructuring features, Before its original attempt, the common framework has resulted in prolonged shutdown of capital formation and has not allowed many in Africa to restructure and move forward on new sound footing and new investment in a timely and fair way. With recent report recommendations, I am assured that we will leave Seville on new footing. The debt for nature, debt for sustainability, and debt for transition structures have also been bogged down by long, cumbersome processes, with few development actors providing the guarantee lip pin that are needed for these structures. We must simplify and speed these debt swaps to reduce these debt burdens. As a bank and as a professional who has only ever represented sovereign sides in restructurings, I want to respectfully oppose those who call for a so-called HIPC II or other euphemisms for scaled, broad-based, and blanket debt forgiveness, as I personally believe that to be a false solution that would lead to less capital flows, not more, less investor confidence, not more. There are other solutions. That said, we must be radical in crowding in development capital through implementation of many of the recommendations discussed over the past few days, from blended finance to improved MDB risk mitigation and regulatory reforms. Efforts from the MDBs to provide more effective risk mitigation tools, like those being taken by MIGA, must continue and be measured and scorecarded. We must acknowledge that the 50 to $70 billion hole in ODA is an additional recent blow to the LICs, to the poorest in the world, and requires a Herculean effort of all those in this room to find funding sources that can offset such impact. The overarching recommendation with which I will conclude today is to leave here and implement. We have failed in so many ways to deliver on the Sustainable Finance Addis Ababa commitments. We have discussed many of these recommendations repeatedly for a decade. Let Seville be the launchpad of action. Thank you.

Right. Thank you so much. And actions are very much what's needed today, not just our 11 actions to unlock sustainable finance and providing the solutions, but the rest of the excellent recommendations and applicable solution that have been there in different aspects on the outcome document. Again, we need to deal with that all as a system. Jay, of course, in his remarks, mentioned something related to the HEPIC initiative. We're the epic moment of the past, but those who have been calling it, reminding us of some global initiatives that worked in the past with solidarity, with political leadership, not to repeat exactly what happened in the past. So there are many solutions. more workable and less demanding when it comes to political leadership. And I think we can take it from there. I'm happy to conclude this part of the discussion. I'm very grateful to our eloquent three speakers and the two excellent discussions. I know that you all had more to say, have been spending your time, not just now, but in the past as well, articulating your understanding, our many ideas on behalf of your institutions and your personal experience, but we are all constrained on time. The time that was mentioned as well by my good friend Axel, that should really be very much guiding us when we are pushing for solutions, not just for debt, but for pushing finance for sustainable development. Having said that, very grateful, and I'm happy to turn now the order of this session back to the co-chair. Thank you so much.

Thank you very much.

I thank the moderator for expertly guiding the discussion. I'd also like to thank our distinguished panelists and discussants for their substantive contributions. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, we will now hear interventions from participants in the roundtable. All participants are invited to speak from their seats. We have a very high number of speakers wishing to make statements in the round table, and as you know, we only have three hours for our deliberations. So as to maximize the time available to us and allow as many participants as possible to take the floor, I would kindly urge all speakers to limit their statements to three minutes. To assist speakers in this regard, a timer has been installed. When the clock signifies that the three minutes have been exhausted, speakers are kindly requested to conclude their statements. Bearing in mind this three-minute limit, I would like to appeal to speakers to deliver their statements at a normal speed so that the interpretation may be provided properly. Delegations wishing to make interventions and who have not previously indicated their intention to do so are kindly requested to approach the Secretariat in the room. I now open the floor for interventions. In this regard, you are encouraged to limit your statement to three minutes, as I already mentioned, so that all requests for the floor can responded to and so that you can deliver your statement. Without further ado, I give the floor to His Excellency the Vice President of the Republic of Botswana.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, esteemed colleagues, I add our voice with humility and with urgency from Botswana, a country that has long valued fiscal discipline and sovereign integrity. But today I speak on behalf of all developing nations who face an unjust paradox. We are asked to grow our economies, build resilience, and deliver on climate action, yet we do so while burdened by a debt architecture that drains our futures to pay for our pasts. Excellencies, let us be clear that this is not just a debt crisis, it is a development crisis. It is a justice crisis. The 2023 UNCTAD Trade and Development Report reveals that between 2010 and 2023, developing countries' total sovereign debt more than doubled from $4.9 trillion to over $11.4 trillion. Debt servicing costs exploded from $1.0 to $1.4 trillion per year, crowding out vital investments in health, education, and climate resilience. This is unsustainable. At the end of 2022, according to the same report, low-income countries were spending on average 22.6% of their export revenues just to service debt. For middle- and low-income countries combined, the burden was 15.7%. This is not a path to prosperity. It is a spiral towards insolvency. Meanwhile, the DEIS report warns that 47 of the 66 most economically vulnerable countries, home to over 1.2 billion people, will face debt insolvency risks within the next five years, largely driven by climate development financing need. It's time to transform the system. I propose three imperatives. First, as urged in the policy submission of the UN Framework Convention on Sovereign Debt, we must establish a statutory, fair, and transparent global mechanism for debt resolution. with automatic standstills during crises, risk sharing clauses for climate shocks, and binding rules for creditor participation. Second, we must redefine debt sustainability. Third, we must scale up innovative instruments like resilience bonds, sustainable development bonds, and sovereign debt swaps mechanisms to create fiscal space for critical investments while reducing the debt burden. To the decision makers in this room, building a development oriented sovereign debt architecture is not just a matter of economics, but a matter of dignity. It is about aligning financial rules of the world with the human values we proclaim. Let Seville be remembered as a place where we begin to redesign a global debt system that empowers growth instead of extracting it, a system that delivers fairness instead of reinforcing asymmetry, a system that reflects not just market logic, but human logic. I thank you.
I thank Vice President of the Republic of Lesotho, and now the floor, His Excellency David Moinina Senghor, Chief Minister of the Republic of Sierra Leone.

Distinguished co-chairs, excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the last decade has taught us hard lessons. The assumption that international capital will naturally flow to developing countries for development has proven flawed. and the drive to finance large scale infrastructure and economic transformation, many of us overlooked the strategic value of mobilizing and managing domestic capital, the urgent reform of global financial architecture and debt management. We acknowledge that, yes, investors seek certainty, yet too often the risks they perceive in our markets are exaggerated and amplified by global credit rating agencies whose assessments frequently fail to reflect our reform trajectories and economic fundamentals. The statistics are sobering. According to the IMF, sub-Saharan African nations pay an average of 155 basis points more than their peers when accessing Eurobond markets between 2014 and 2021. That premium is not just a data point. It is the price of inequality. It is the cost of outdated narratives and institutional asymmetry, which lead African countries into more debt, and it is unfair. The implication is a real and painful constraint on our capacity to build more schools, power more hospitals, provide clean water, and meet our sustainable development goals for our citizens. In that spirit, allow me to offer three key recommendations. First, we must restore credibility and fairness in the global credit rating system. The establishment of the African Credit Rating Agency is a welcome and long overdue response to systemic bias. We must all commit to supporting and strengthening it. Second, we must redefine liquidity metrics and adopt broader criteria that reflect emerging regional realities. As Africa advances the African Continental Free Trade Area, We are already witnessing increased inter-African trade and improved fiscal coordination. We need metrics that recognize these gains and promote confidence rather than distortion. Third, we must build lasting institutional capacity to manage public debt responsibly. Under the leadership of His Excellency President Julius Maada Bio, and with support from the World Bank and IMF, Sierra Leone is implementing a public debt management strategy within a wider public debt financial management architecture. More of this needs to be supported across the continent. And closing, Excellencies, Sierra Leone aligns fully with the Cape Town Declaration and its vision for a just, inclusive, and development-oriented debt architecture. Let this conference mark the moment we shifted from extractive terms to equitable partnerships, from opaque assessments to transparent accountability, and from fragmented efforts to collective resolve. Together, let us build a debt architecture that does not punish vulnerability, but instead enables dignity see development and the future that our people deserve. When we do so, together, we will deliver a more just world. I thank you.
I thank the Minister of the Republic of Sierra Leone, and I now give the floor to their Excellency Ines Maria Chapna, the Deputy Prime Minister of the Republic of Cuba.

Good afternoon. Thank you very much, Mr. Co-Chair, distinguished panelists. The current system of sovereign debt was designed to fail developing countries. This system is obsolete and unfair. It continues to serve the interests of creditors over and above the needs of our nations. In 2023, approximately 40% of developing countries suffered serious indebtedness issues, even though these countries only represent 2.5% of the global economy. They are home to 15% of the global population and 40% of all of the peoples living in conditions of extreme poverty. These groups also include more than half of the 50 countries that are most vulnerable to climate change. The FFD4 conference should strive to ensure a debt architecture based on three pillars. Firstly, binding debt clauses. Any restructuring or loan should include the automatic suspension of payment where there are health or climate crises. They should also link debt service to true economic growth and not to austerity. Secondly, there should be a multilateral mechanism under the UN that is not in exclusive formats such as the G20, which favours profit over other interests and should ensure the participation of all creditors, including the private sector and the significant participation of countries of the South, restructuring of multilateral development banks to improve their lending conditions, donations for countries in extreme climatic stress, particularly small island developing states. Three, innovative financing across the cycle, including debt for investment swaps, special drawing rights from the IMF assigned on the development needs of southern countries and not obsolete quotas. In essence, the world cannot continue to allow a system that ensures that the majority of developing countries pay more on servicing their debt than schools and hospitals. They plunge our people into suffering and ignoring 70% of low-income countries that are over-indebted. We aspire to ensure that this international conference sets the pace for a new international framework in which debt is no longer an obstacle to development. Thank you.

Thanks, Deputy Prime Minister of the Republic of Cuba. Now the floor.

And I get the floor to His Excellency Gustavo Ochoa, Minister of State of Foreign Affairs for Palau.

Thank you, co-chairs. Co-chairs, I have the honor to deliver these remarks on behalf of the Alliance of Small Island States, the AOSIS. Small island developing states are facing deep and protracted debt distress. We are caught in a vicious cycle where climate shocks force us to borrow repeatedly, often at high cost, just to rebuild. This diverts already scarce resources away from our long-term development. It is a debt we accumulate not because of fiscal management, but because we are on the front lines of a crisis we did not create. In this regard, AOSIS wishes to highlight three urgent priorities. First, we call for support to fully operationalize the SIDS Debt Sustainability Support Service. This is a proposal built by SIDS for SIDS. It offers independent, transparent assessments of debt sustainability, incorporating our real vulnerabilities and not just income metrics. It is flexible, scalable, and tailored to the evolving risk our countries face. The DSSS would empower governments and creditors alike with better data, tailored support, and enable early interventions before crisis erupts. Second, we urge the expansion and adaptation of the G20 common framework. to explicitly include SIDS. The framework in its current form was not designed with our economies in mind. We need the common framework to reflect the specific characteristics of small island developing economies and circumstances, offering timely, fair, and coordinated instructions with clear pathways to restore debt sustainability. An accelerated track for SIDS within the common framework could be a game changer. Third, We emphasize the importance of the intergovernmental process on debt as outlined in the Seville outcome. This must be the space where comprehensive reform of the sovereign debt architecture is advanced. In that context, AOC strongly supports the development of an international sovereign debt instrument that is legally grounded and ensures predictable, inclusive, and fair debt resolution processes. For CDS, such an instrument could finally align the global financial system with the realities of our economies and the shocks we face. This is not a technical exercise. It is a question of justice. Let us move decisively. If we are serious about building a fair and resilient international financial system, we must act now. Thank you.

Muy las gracias.

I thank the Minister of State for Palau. And I now give the floor to His Excellency, the Minister of Finance and Economic Development and Investment of Zimbabwe.

Thank you, co-chair. My delegation welcomes this roundtable, which focuses on debt issues, because we are laden with debt. and it is slowing down our economic development path. We're in a situation like most other African countries, where debt repayments now exceed what we are outlaying for health, for infrastructure development, education, and to deal with climate resilience issues. We are doing our part to deal with this issue, to confront it. We have launched an arrears clearance, debt relief, and restructuring strategy. But also growth over the last seven years is a system in lowering the debt to GDP ratio from as high as 80% and down to 45%. But in order to address this debt challenge more broadly, a combination of national initiatives and enabling global environment which prioritizes sustainable development will be critical. To this end, we call upon the following. One, the introduction of an in duplum rule for sovereign debt the same way that it exists for commercial debt, making sure that the debt does not exceed the initial borrowed amount. And secondly, to work with credit rating agencies for them to adopt more flexible methodologies to positively support those countries that are in voluntary debt restructuring modes. Third is to support countries in making use of state contingent debt instruments, blended finance, credit enhancement instruments, and also to encourage SDR recycling in a way that will lower borrowing costs. We also call on AIDA deputies and ADF deputies to seriously consider set asides in their resource allocation in order to support those countries that wish to clear IFI debt. We should also support those countries that seek to build sovereign wealth funds as a way to build a sovereign balance sheet and not just to focus on debt, but also to focus on the asset side of that balance sheet. To conclude, I wish to reiterate that debt restructuring remains one of the most significant threats to sustainable development in developing countries. The legacy of FfD4 will depend on how decisively we address this pressing challenge. We should therefore harness this opportunity to reaffirm our commitment to address the debt distress affecting many of our countries and to support the accelerated implementation of the SDGs, building upon the outcomes of this severe consensus. I thank you.
I'd like to thank the Minister of Finance of Zimbabwe, and I would like to give the floor to the Minister of Finance and the Economy of Mali.

Distinguished co-chairs, ladies and gentlemen, all protocols observed. In Mali, outstanding debt stands at 49.7% of GDP. Debt service eats up 33% of our tax revenue. The share of bilateral and multilateral partners is increasingly falling and now stands at 51.6% of debt. Government has been stressing rigorous and transparent public debt management in keeping with our long-term vision, Mali 2063. This vision is underpinned by the principles of sovereignty, good governance, and sets forth the reforms necessary for growing our domestic resources, digitalization, and a revision of various regulations. What's more is Malawi is prioritizing financing for strategic sectors which drive sustainable growth, have a positive impact on our people, as well as investment in security and the fight against the effects of climate change. Implementing the aforementioned vision means ensuring that Malawi continues to have a moderate debt burden and ensuring that our debt is sustainable. evidenced by recent reports, 2024 and 2025, from the World Bank and the IMF, respectively. Nonetheless, a drop in concessional financing and the imposition of non-economic conditions have been restricting financing. These conditions are being applied by partners, forcing us to resort to increasingly expensive commercial debt. And this expense is often divorced from the regional economic environment. Let's recall that developed countries have committed to allocate 0.7% of their GDP to ODA, but this commitment has not been upheld. Thus, the share of debt servicing has been diminishing our fiscal space, diminishing our ability to spend on strategic sectors such as defense and high growth sectors and human development. We need new sovereign debt architecture. which should strengthen and make more flexible financing mechanisms for fragile countries, introduce innovative mechanisms so as to avoid an accumulation of arrears, and take into account specific characteristics and visions of countries. I thank you for your kind attention.
I thank His Excellency, and I give the floor to the Minister of Finance from the Central African Republic.

Excellencies, co-chairs, ladies and gentlemen, the Central African Republic has experienced difficult times with several decades of human and other crises, which has had a considerable impact on our economy. the loss of around seven budgetary points of GDP over the last few years as a result of geopolitical tensions has forced us to compensate them by extremely onerous financing from the lending markets. The latest debt sustainability analysis by the IMF shows that we have a level of indebtedness of 58%, which is below the regional threshold of 70%. However, our country ranks among those with a high level debt distress, both exterior and external and global, because our debt service represents 34% of our budgetary income, considerably hampering our ability to invest in basic social services. So we call for an urgent restructuring of our debt, as well as the G20 common framework to make it more effective, more swift and transparent, particularly through the suspension of debt service through all countries entering restructuring of the common framework, the adoption of an integrated approach between public and private creditors, and a restructuring of multilateral and bilateral debts, the development of an equal treatment formula to reduce technical disputes and speed up restructurings. We also call for the establishment of financing and debt management mechanisms which take into account the vulnerabilities of developing countries such as the CAR that are facing exogenous and endogenous shocks. It's important to develop resilient tools to, for instance, include debt suspension clauses where there are natural disasters or major crises. The restructuring of the IMF and World Bank Group debt sustainability analyses is important so that it should be mainly focused on solvency. We should ensure widespread investment in human capital and socioeconomic infrastructure. Development-oriented debt should allow us to access long-term finance on exceptional concessional conditions and low-risk conditions. The international community's support should help us focus on climate and other risks while also aligned with our sustainable development goals, the sustainable without forgetting the assets of, for instance, our young people and our women.

Thank you.
I thank His Excellency, and I now give the floor to the Minister of Economy and Finance of Burundi. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Co-Chair. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, distinguished participants, Burundi is delighted to be partaking In this roundtable, much like other developing countries, Burundi has a lot of public debt, which is hampering our ability to invest in key sectors for development. In 2023, our public debt stood at 48% of our GDP. Debt service stood at roughly 20% of our government revenues. While manageable, our budgetary room for maneuver is limited. Having said that, we don't think debt should be simply a burden. It should be a lever for development if it is well managed and placed squarely within a fairer international financial architecture. For this reason, Burundi strongly supports the establishment of a multilateral framework for addressing debt, and this under the auspices of the United Nations. Such a framework would allow for swift and tailored adaptation to the needs of the most vulnerable countries, all the while respecting the need to achieve the SDGs. We are in favor of contingency clauses especially debt suspension clauses in case of endogenous shocks striking, for instance, natural disasters, pandemics, or other climate crises. This will help to bolster our resilience, the resilience of our budgets, without circumscribing our ability to meet the pressing needs of our people. Moreover, we call for a revision of the credit rating agencies' credit assessment systems. They continue to penalize developing countries, resulting in high interest rates. And this even when our economic fundamentals are very similar to those of countries with high ratings. We need to invest not just in the SDGs, but we also need to ensure that risk assessments take these into account. We welcome an African credit rating agency being established. We believe this is an important stepping stone on the way to restoring the financial and information-based sovereignty of the continent. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, today, more than ever, we need an international financial system which supports our development priorities, rather than one which contradicts or ignores these very priorities. The time is now. Waiting until tomorrow would mean we'd be too late. As for Burundi, we'd like to reiterate our commitment to using debt in a responsible fashion. However, we also call for debt reform in the spirit of solidarity and economic justice. I thank you for listening to me so graciously.
I thank the distinguished representative of Burundi. I now have the honor of giving the floor to the IMF.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chair, and thank you for the opportunity to speak. It has been expressed by many speakers before me in a more eloquent manner than I could. We are in a situation which is different from the situation that led to the HIPC initiative, but we cannot remain passive and we need to act. Many countries are struggling with high interest costs and refinancing needs that constrain their ability to finance critical spending such as education, health, infrastructure. And some countries are or could find themselves in a situation of unsustainable debt for which efficient and timely restructuring processes are needed. We have seen progress in improving restructuring processes, in particular under the common framework. And the work at the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable, which we are pushing with the World Bank and the G20 presidency, this year South Africa, is helping, including the so-called restructuring playbook that the GSDR published in April, which we believe is an important resource for countries considering a restructuring. But definitely, there is still much more work to be done. And the civil commitment includes helpful and important elements in that regard. The IMF will continue its strong engagement, helping member countries and the international community address their challenges and promote macroeconomic and financial stability, as it is a necessary condition and enabler for sustainable growth and development. We will do so through our policy advice, based on our near-universal membership and 80 years of experience; our support for building institutional capacity in our areas of expertise, which include, of course, fiscal policies and debt management, among others; and through providing financial support where needed to help countries address balance of payment problems. We will also continue to actively support restructuring processes, both for individual restructuring and to promote improvements, including further work at the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable. We have put proposals on the table, and Mr. Moieldin, the enlargement of the common framework to middle-income countries or finding a way to have collective restructuring for those countries is something that both the Bank and the IMF have officially supported. And we will continue our work jointly with the World Bank to help countries faced with liquidity challenges to help mobilize resources and implement domestic reforms and provide external financing as appropriate. We will also continue to review our tools, including the debt sustainability analysis. We are jointly undertaking with the World Bank the review of the debt sustainability analysis for low-income countries and working as well for market access countries. And we will continue our contribution to the collective efforts to improve debt transparency and the accuracy of debt data. Thank you very much.
Okay.
I thank the Minister of Mauritania. I give the floor to the Vice Minister of Development of the Netherlands.

Chair and distinguished excellencies, thank you for facilitating this platform, a burning platform indeed, as it is confirmed once more today. I want to make three points. First, on transparency. In the Netherlands, we have a saying that literally translates to, "Trust arrives on foot and departs on horseback," and can be best summarized as follows, "Trust is hard to gain and easy to lose." This saying effectively summarizes the view of the Netherlands that debt transparency should be a primary focus in improving the sovereign debt architecture. Without transparency, trust is hard to build. Without trust, financing will dry up. Without financing, the SDGs and climate action will continue to stay out of reach. In this sense, debt transparency should remain a key pillar, or even radical transparency, as Axel von Trotsenburg just put it. After all, public debt is public, and citizens all over the world have the right to know how governments and politicians are financing their plans and programs. In this light, we intend to support initiatives that support debt transparency, from capacity development programs to knowledge hubs, and we always advocate for policies that reward transparency. CSOs, press, and parliaments should be enabled to play their roles in this respect. Second, debt resolution. Improving the debt resolution architecture is another key pillar that should be addressed. As an international community, it is our responsibility to ensure that countries in debt distress that operate with good faith are supported and can count on a predictable and speedy process to resolve their debt overhang. Ensuring that improvements are made to the common framework, expanding its eligibility and enhancing its efficiency is a good step in the right direction. We very much welcome the inclusion of language on such an ambition in the Compromiso de Sevilla. Third and last, currency risk. Wherever possible, unsustainable debts should be prevented. Initiatives that reduce currency risk, for instance through local currency lending or hedging currency risk, should be embraced and scaled up. Dutch TCX is a good example. Chairs, your Excellencies, debt stress is high. We have a joint responsibility to come to a resolve. After sharing our views today, we need to find solutions tomorrow, building up on what works. Thank you.
I thank the Vice-Minister of Development of the Netherlands. I now give the floor to Qatar.

Excellencies, I'm pleased to represent the Qatar Fund for Development and to share our experience in advancing responsible sustainable development finance. QFFD operates with strategic alignment to Qatar's national priorities while maintaining operational independence. We work closely with the Ministry of Finance to ensure that our financing instrument, whether grants, concessional loan, or blended mechanism, are fiscally sound, aligned with long-term development goals and concept to global challenges. QFFD is currently undergoing a strategic shift from a model focused on traditional grants to one that emphasizes concessional finance and blended approaches. This evolution is rooted in the belief that enduring development challenges require equally enduring financial tools. that preserve capital, promote co-financing, and reinforce fiscal discipline, while enabling countries to invest in long-term priorities. We see concessional financing not just as a means of reducing borrowing costs, but as a catalyst to unlock additional resources, enhancing debt sustainability, and create space for effective planning and delivery in fragile context or where markets fall short. We combine with this with targeted grant supports to address urgent needs, debt sustainability and transparency remain core to our operation.
